Keeps apart from s9e05 (named once): no lost decision, no fuse, none of its anchors. Keeps apart from a5e03: faithfulness is recalled; the lesson is how it was reported. Timeline: assistant live Monday 2 November 2026 with the staff check holding every vegan or allergy answer (staff read the bottle's back label, then approve or correct and send; a corrected wrong-year reply went out corrected and nobody told the engineer). Wednesday 18 November: her 50 questions, one per wine, written by her from the sheets about what changed since the year before, run and marked. Friday 20 November: rehearsed three-question demo (all three among the 33 right-sheet, faithful answers), then the report: page 1 'Faithfulness 96% (48 of 50)'; page 2 'Right sheet found: 34 of 50', 'Right answers: 33 of 50'. Friday 4 December: the owner switches the staff check off in the afternoon; newsletter at 18:00 'Our assistant is 96% accurate: ask it anything', from page 1's 48 of 50; the winter tasting; 20:40 a guest reads 'Yes, the 2022 is vegan' holding the 2022 bottle labelled 'Contains: egg' (answered from the 2021 sheet); after closing at 21:30 she checks the log's 20 questions: 13 right. Given data, all in the sim: her 50 split 33 right-sheet faithful right (14 vegan or allergy), 1 right-sheet not faithful, 15 wrong-year faithful (6 vegan or allergy), 1 wrong-year not faithful; tonight's 20 split 13 (5 vegan or allergy), 1, 5 (3), 1 (1); the owner's 10 split 7 (2) right and 3 wrong-year faithful (2); busy Saturday 12 December: 120 questions, 30 vegan or allergy, staff check about 60 a day. Meeting Monday 7 December 10:00; corrected newsletter Tuesday 8 December. Cold case: 2 months later, events from December to Monday 1 February 2027. Sources read 16 October 2026; the ISO 9001 and SOC 2 pages are third-party listings; the ISO/IEC 42001 page is a national standards body's catalogue entry.
title: Writing It Down

post.author: u/sheet_by_year_liutgard
post.title: I wrote the eval report for a wine merchant's assistant. Tonight, at his tasting, a guest read out 'the 2022 is vegan', holding a 2022 bottle whose label says 'Contains: egg'.

blocks.text: I'm a forward-deployed engineer. A consultancy sends me inside a client's business to build and launch its AI (artificial intelligence) system. My client: a wine merchant, two shops, 900 wines.

Every wine has one sheet per vintage, the year its grapes were picked. A sheet lists grapes, food to serve it with, vegan or not, and allergens: ingredients some people react to, like egg. The 2021 and 2022 Brackenlea Red sheets share a name except for the year.

His assistant, on the website and the shops' tablets, went live on Monday 2 November. A language model, a program that writes text, answers in three steps. First, the assistant finds the sheet whose words best match the question. Then it hands that sheet and the question to the model. Last, the model writes an answer from it.

Answers about vegan or allergies waited for a person: the staff check. A member of staff read the bottle's back label, then approved the reply, or corrected it and sent it. Other answers went out in seconds.

On Wednesday 18 November I tested it. I wrote 50 questions, one per wine, each about what changed since the year before, ran them and marked every answer. A test like that is an eval; its write-up for a client is an eval report.
Each number is a metric: one thing, counted the same way every time. Right sheet found: the right wine and year? Right answers: true for the bottle asked about?
The third was faithfulness: does every claim in the answer appear on the sheet it was handed, whichever sheet that was?

On Friday 20 November I gave the owner a demo, a live run in front of him. We'd rehearsed it: I picked three questions, ran them that morning, walked him through them, then asked them again in the meeting. All three came back right. Then I handed him the report:

blocks.title: EVAL REPORT, ASSISTANT, 20 NOVEMBER
items: Page 1, in large type: Faithfulness 96% (48 of 50)
blocks.sig: Two pages, handed over after the demo.

blocks.text: Tonight, Friday 4 December, was his winter tasting. At 18:00 the newsletter went to every customer: 'Our assistant is 96% accurate: ask it anything.' My page 1, 48 of 50. That afternoon he'd switched the staff check off. I stood by the tasting tablet, where guests typed questions.
At 20:40 a guest read the tablet aloud: 'Yes, the 2022 is vegan.' She was holding the 2022 bottle. Its back label says 'Contains: egg'.

It had answered from the 2021 sheet. After closing at 21:30 I checked tonight's 20 questions in its log, the record of every question, sheet and answer, against the back labels. Each line: group, count, how many right.

right sheet, faithful        13   13
right sheet, not faithful     1    0
wrong year, faithful          5    0
wrong year, not faithful      1    0
tonight                      20   13 of 20
Four of the seven wrong answers were about vegan or allergies, and went straight to guests. Then I re-read my marks for the 50.

blocks.label: my_50_remarked.png

diagram.aria: My drawing of the 50 eval questions, marked on Wednesday 18 November. Top: my 50 questions, one per wine, written from the sheets. Middle: the right sheet came back for 34, where the three demo questions all sit; the wrong year's sheet, same name, came back for 16. Bottom, under the 34: 33 faithful and right, 1 not faithful and wrong. Under the 16: 15 faithful to the other year's sheet and wrong, 1 not faithful and wrong. Faithful: 33 plus 15 is 48 of 50. Right answers: 33 of 50.

notes.text: Marked Wednesday 18 November, re-read Friday 4 December

blocks.caption: Drawn at 22:15 from my marking sheet. The right sheet came back for 34 of the 50, and the rehearsed demo's three questions were all among them. For 16, the other year's sheet came first. 33 answers stuck to the right sheet and were right; 15 stuck faithfully to the wrong year's sheet and were wrong. Two answers added something their sheet didn't say.

blocks.text: Every number I printed was true. Until tonight, staff corrected each wrong-year vegan or allergy answer from the back label, and nobody told me.

On 20 November he'd asked one thing: can it answer my customers without my staff? In my notebook: what did he think 48 of 50 meant? We meet Monday at 10:00. What should I change before I reissue the report, sending it again corrected?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at that tasting is haunted, and every number you printed was true. A report is read from the top down. One idea for later: for a client, a short paper that lists the decisions they must make, each with its options and what it costs, is called a design doc. And forward-deployed interviews have a presentation round, a stage where you show results to a pretend client. It tests this night. Two questions. What did the owner ask you before the demo, in his words? And who wrote the 50 questions, and from what?

replies.author: u/sheet_by_year_liutgard
replies.text: His words: 'Can it answer my customers without my staff?' The 50 were mine, one per wine, written from the sheets about what changed since the year before. The three demo questions were ones I'd already seen come back right. And the back label is the producer's own wording: where a labelling rule applies, it's the label that counts, not the assistant. Not legal advice.

comments.author: u/page_one_said_it_bozena
comments.text: Faithfulness 96% (48 of 50) is what your own report says; the client only repeated it. Page 1, large type, your number. Don't walk in on Monday taking it back. Make it true instead: two of your 50 answers weren't faithful, so tighten the model's instructions until it writes only what the sheet says. 50 of 50, and nobody can call the newsletter a stretch.

replies.author: u/sheet_by_year_liutgard
replies.text: Both of those two were wrong answers, yes.

replies.author: u/page_one_said_it_bozena
replies.text: Then fix those two. The other 48 stuck to the sheet.

comments.author: u/rehearse_it_vlasta
comments.text: Clients buy confidence. Your demo went perfectly, and that's what he remembers. Next time, demo only questions you've run beforehand, so nothing surprises him in the room, and put the hard cases at the back of the report.

replies.author: u/sheet_by_year_liutgard
replies.text: All three on 20 November were run beforehand.

comments.author: u/hold_them_all_svatava
comments.text: One wrong allergy answer got out. Hold every answer for staff, not just vegan and allergy ones, until you've tested again. Nothing wrong reaches a customer that way.

replies.author: u/sheet_by_year_liutgard
replies.text: On a busy Saturday the assistant gets about 120 questions, 30 of them about vegan or allergies. Staff can check about 60 a day between customers.

reply.prompt: The owner meets me at 10:00 on Monday 7 December, and the newsletter has gone out. What should I change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Raise faithfulness to 50 of 50 so answers stick to the sheet found.
options.part2: On Monday I left the report as it was and tightened the model's instructions: write only what the sheet says. I re-ran my 50 on Tuesday 8 December. Faithfulness: 50 of 50. The one right-sheet answer that had added a claim was now right, so right answers rose to 34 of 50. The 16 wrong-year answers stuck to their sheets, every word, and all 16 were still wrong. The owner read '50 of 50' and left the staff check off; the newsletter stayed. I replayed the tasting's 20 questions: 14 right, and the same 4 wrong vegan or allergy answers went straight to the asker, now perfectly faithful to the wrong year's sheet.
options.senior: Faithfulness measures whether an answer sticks to the sheet it was handed, not whether that was the right sheet. Raising it to 50 of 50 can fix at most the one right-sheet answer that strayed, so right answers stop at 34, the number of right sheets found. The 16 wrong-year answers only become more faithful to the wrong year. And the real problem is untouched: the owner read the wrong number first, and a bigger version of that number makes the misreading worse.

options.text: Send a longer report that lists every metric, so nothing is left out.
options.verdict: More numbers, the same first line
options.part2: On Monday I sent a longer report: every metric I could count, each on its own line, in the same size type. Faithfulness came first again, because it had been first before: 96% (48 of 50). Right answers, 33 of 50, sat on page 3, between right sheet found and how long replies took. The owner read page 1, said 'so nothing has changed', and kept the staff check off and the newsletter up. I replayed the tasting's 20 questions with the check off: 13 right, and the same 4 wrong vegan or allergy answers reached the asker.
options.senior: More numbers don't change which number is read first. A client reads from the top and stops when something answers his question; a list of every metric gives him more to choose from, and he takes the biggest. Choose the one number that answers the client's question, lead with it, and define the others beside their numbers. Completeness belongs in an appendix, not in the headline.

options.text: Reissue it led by right answers, 33 of 50, and restore the check.
options.part2: At 10:00 on Monday 7 December I gave the owner the reissued report. Page 1, in large type: Right answers: 33 of 50, true for the bottle asked about. Beside each number, one sentence on what it counts: right sheet found, 34 of 50; faithfulness, 48 of 50, meaning the answer stuck to the sheet it was handed, right year or not. Who wrote the questions: me, one per wine, about what changed since the year before. Three failures in full, the 2022 vegan question first. What the number does not mean: it is not yet a number on customers' own questions. And in bold: keep the staff check on vegan and allergy answers until right answers reach a level we agree, on 50 questions from customers' own messages. He switched the check back on at 10:40. Then he picked 10 questions himself, on the spot, and we ran them: 7 of 10 right, 10 of 10 faithful. All 3 wrong ones came from the wrong year; the 2 about vegan or allergies were held, and staff corrected them; the third was a food question. On Tuesday 8 December the newsletter said: our assistant answers from each wine's sheet; in our latest test it gave 33 right answers out of 50; staff check every vegan and allergy answer.
options.senior: Lead with the number that answers the client's question. His was whether customers get right answers, so the headline is right answers, 33 of 50. Define each metric in one plain sentence beside its number, say what the questions were and who wrote them, show three failures, say what the number does not mean, and end with the recommendation. Demo on questions the client picks on the day: his 10 showed 7 right and 10 faithful, the same gap in front of him, and he watched the check catch two. A correct report led by the wrong number answers the wrong question.

options.text: Put a staff check on every answer until the next eval is finished.
options.verdict: Safe, and slow on busy days
options.part2: On Monday I asked the owner to hold every answer for staff until I had run the next eval. He agreed, and nothing wrong reached a customer that week. On Saturday 12 December, the busiest day of the month, the assistant took 120 questions. Staff checked 60 between customers; the other 60 waited until the next morning, including customers buying gifts that afternoon. The report still led with faithfulness, 48 of 50, the newsletter still stood, and I hadn't booked the next eval. On Monday the owner asked when he could switch the check off.
options.senior: Holding every answer is the honest safe choice: nothing wrong reaches a customer, and it buys time. But it costs the speed the assistant was built for: on a busy Saturday half the replies waited until the next morning. And it leaves the misreading in place. The report and the newsletter still lead with 48 of 50 faithful, so the check comes off the day the eval is 'finished'. Hold what can hurt, the vegan and allergy answers; fix the report the client reads; and agree in writing when the check may come off.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the tasting was haunted. The report was correct, but it led with faithfulness, which counts answers that stick to the sheet found, right year or not: 33 right plus 15 faithful to the wrong year made 48 of 50. The owner's question was whether customers get right answers, 33 of 50, so he read 48 as accuracy, told his customers so, and switched off the staff check that had been catching the wrong-year answers.

steps.title: Three metrics, one question.
steps.text: Each answer passes two steps. First, the assistant finds a sheet: the right one for 34 of 50, the other year's for 16. Second, the model writes from that sheet. Of the 34, 33 answers stuck to the sheet and were right; 1 added a claim the sheet didn't hold, and was wrong. Of the 16, 15 stuck faithfully to the wrong year's sheet, so they were wrong; 1 wasn't faithful either. Faithful: 33 + 15 = 48 of 50. Right: 33 of 50. What can go wrong: faithfulness can't see whether the sheet was the right one, so it stays high while the finding step fails. Even at 50 of 50 faithful, right answers stop at 34, the right sheets found. a5e03 taught faithfulness; the lesson here is how it was reported.

steps.title: Finding a sheet when two years share a name.
steps.text: The finding step runs in three steps. First, it compares the question's words with every sheet's words. Second, it scores each sheet by how close the two are. Third, it hands the top sheet to the model. The 2021 and 2022 Brackenlea Red sheets share every word of their name except the year, so their scores sit almost level, and for 16 of 50 questions the other year came first. What can go wrong: a year is one word among many, and closeness scores barely notice it, much as a3e07 (when retrieval lies) found with names kept only in a header. a5e02 showed how to score this step; here it was scored correctly, 34 of 50, on page 2. The later fix is to match the year exactly before scoring.

steps.title: Why it never showed before.
steps.text: From Monday 2 November every answer about vegan or allergies was held. First, the reply waited. Then a member of staff read the bottle's back label. Last, they approved the reply, or corrected it and sent it. A wrong-year answer went out corrected, and nobody told the engineer, because a corrected reply looked like the check doing its job. The three demo questions were all among the 33 right answers, so the demo never met the wrong year. What can go wrong: on Friday 4 December the check was switched off, and that night 4 wrong vegan or allergy answers went straight to guests. The 3 other wrong answers, about food or grapes, would have gone out with the check on too.

steps.title: Writing it down for a client.
steps.text: A client's eval report runs in this order. First, the number that answers the client's question: right answers, 33 of 50. Second, each metric defined in one plain sentence beside its number. Third, what the questions were and who wrote them: 50, one per wine, written by the engineer from the sheets. Fourth, three failures in full, such as the 2022 vegan question answered from the 2021 sheet. Fifth, what the number does not mean: 48 of 50 faithful is not 48 right. Last, the recommendation: keep the staff check on vegan and allergy answers until right answers reach an agreed level on customers' own questions. A demo runs on questions the client picks on the day, and a design doc for a client lists the decisions the client must make. What can go wrong: a correct report led by the wrong number answers the wrong question.

diagram.aria: The reissued report, drawn as the order it is read in. Top row, left to right: the owner's question, can it answer customers alone; the headline, right answers 33 of 50, first and in large type; each metric defined beside its number, faithfulness 48 not meaning 48 right; the recommendation, the staff check stays on vegan and allergy answers. Bottom row: who wrote the questions, the engineer, 50, one per wine; three failures, wrong-year answers such as the 2022 answered from the 2021 sheet; what the number does not mean, not yet customers' own questions; and the next demo, 10 questions the owner picks on the day.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: the owner's question picks the headline, each metric is defined beside its number, and the report ends with the recommendation. The bottom row is what sits under the headline: who wrote the questions, three failures in full, what the number does not mean, and a demo on questions he picks.

fix.title: The fix: lead with right answers, define every metric, restore the check
fix.text: Reissue the report with the number that answers the owner's question as its headline: right answers, 33 of 50, true for the bottle asked about. Define each metric in one plain sentence beside its number, so faithfulness, 48 of 50, reads as 'stuck to the sheet it was handed', not 'right'. Say the questions were 50, one per wine, written by the engineer from the sheets. Show three wrong-year failures in full. Say what 33 of 50 does not mean: not yet a number on customers' own questions. End with the recommendation in bold: the staff check stays on vegan and allergy answers until right answers reach a level agreed in writing. Ask the owner to correct the newsletter, and run the next demo on 10 questions he picks on the day.

limits: 33 of 50 comes from questions the engineer wrote, each about what changed since the year before: harder on the year than most customers' questions, perhaps easier on others. It isn't yet a number on customers' own questions, and the report must say so.

Restoring the check stops wrong vegan and allergy answers, not wrong food or grape answers: tonight 3 of the 7 wrong would still have gone out. The finding step still needs its own fix: match the year exactly before scoring.
A client can still repeat a correct report wrongly. Ask to see anything public that quotes it, such as a newsletter, before it goes out.

explain.seniorTake: An eval report is read from the top, and its first number becomes the client's answer to whatever he asked. So find his question before you write: here, can it answer my customers without my staff? Lead with the number that answers it, define each metric beside its number, say who wrote the questions and from what, show three failures, say what the number does not mean, and end with a recommendation he can act on. Demo on questions the client picks on the day, never only rehearsed ones. A design doc for a client works the same way: the decisions he must make, each with its options and costs. The presentation round of a forward-deployed interview loop tests this skill: expect 'present your eval results to a client: which number do you lead with?'

realWorld.title: Model cards: what it is for, and how it was tested
realWorld.text: Mitchell and colleagues' Model Cards for Model Reporting (FAT* 2019) says: Model cards also disclose the context in which models are intended to be used, and the same sentence goes on to details of the performance evaluation procedures. For the merchant, the intended use was answering customers about one bottle and year; the procedure was 50 questions written by the engineer from the sheets.

realWorld.title: Model cards: results across conditions
realWorld.text: The same abstract says: Model cards are short documents accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions. Here the conditions that matter are the right sheet found, 33 of 34 right, and the wrong year found, 0 of 16 right.

realWorld.title: Ragas: what faithfulness measures
realWorld.text: The Ragas documentation says: The Faithfulness metric measures how factually consistent a response is with the retrieved context. The retrieved context is the sheet the assistant found, whichever year it was.

realWorld.title: Ragas: faithful means supported, not right
realWorld.text: It also says: A response is considered faithful if all its claims can be supported by the retrieved context. The 2022 vegan answer was supported by the 2021 sheet, so it was faithful, and wrong.

realWorld.title: ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.5: documented information
realWorld.text: A third-party listing of the standard's clauses gives 7.5 Documented Information, with 7.5.2 Creating and updating and 7.5.3 Control of documented information. A reissued report is an update: it needs a version and a note of what changed.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023: AI management systems
realWorld.text: The catalogue entry says: This document is intended for use by an organization providing or using products or services that utilize AI systems. A merchant running an assistant and a consultancy building one are both such users; check the standard's own clauses on verification and reporting in your copy.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 CC2.3: communication with external parties
realWorld.text: A third-party listing gives the criterion as: The entity communicates with external parties regarding matters affecting the functioning of internal control. The staff check is a control, and what the client was told about it decided whether it stayed on.

asked: Present your eval results to a client: which number do you lead with?
Your client has quoted a metric from your report as accuracy. What do you do?
interview.answer: I start from the client's question, in his words, before I choose a headline. If he asks whether the assistant can answer customers without staff, I lead with right answers: how many were true for the thing asked about, out of how many. I define every other metric in one plain sentence beside its number, so faithfulness reads as 'stuck to the document it was handed', not 'right'. I say what the questions were and who wrote them, show three failures in full, say what the number does not mean, and end with a recommendation. If he has already quoted the wrong number, I reissue the report the same day, ask him to correct anything public, and put back any safety check he removed because of it. Then I run the next demo on questions he picks on the day. At a wine merchant that meant 33 of 50 right as the headline, 48 of 50 faithful explained beside it, and the staff check back on vegan and allergy answers.

atWork: Look for an eval headline a client could read as accuracy. It is a common pattern: the report is correct, but its first number measures something narrower than the client's question, such as faithfulness, and the client repeats it as 'accurate'. Ask four things. What did the client ask, in his words, and does page 1 answer it? Is each metric defined in one plain sentence beside its number? Does the report say who wrote the questions, show failures and say what the number does not mean? And did any safety check get switched off because of the report? Its Dead Letter partner, s9e05 Write It Down, writes for the team; this case writes for a client. Build Night: X2 'Evals on 50 past incidents' asks for this case's metric definitions beside each number, but it unlocks on a5e02, a5e03 and a5e04, not on this case, and this case feeds no milestone. Standards-readiness note, as these apply to you and not legal advice: where an organisation works to ISO 9001:2015, clause 7.5 (documented information) is likely to expect reports like this to be created, updated and controlled, so a reissue carries a version and a note of what changed; where ISO/IEC 42001:2023 applies, its verification and reporting expectations for AI systems are likely to cover how eval results reach the client; and where a SOC 2 report covers the service, CC2.3 (communication with external parties) is likely to cover what a client is told about a control such as the staff check. Where a wine-labelling or allergen rule applies, the bottle's label, not the assistant, is what counts. Building this in now costs far less than rewriting reports at audit time.

recall.prompt: A colleague built a refunds helper for a bike shop. Page 1 of her report says 'Answer relevance 47 of 50'. The manager has told staff the helper is 'nearly always correct' and stopped checking the refunds it approves. What should she do with her report?

keyIdeas.idea: Lead with the number that answers the manager's question: how many answers were right for the case asked about
Define each metric in a plain sentence beside its number, and say what it does not mean
Show failures and end with a recommendation: restore the check until right answers reach an agreed level

recall.model: Reissue it with the number that answers the manager's question first: right answers, how many refunds the helper got right out of 50, as the headline. Define each metric in one plain sentence beside its number, and say what answer relevance does not mean: on topic is not the same as right. Say who wrote the questions, show three failures in full, and end with the recommendation: restore the check on refunds until right answers reach an agreed level on customers' own requests.

recall.prompt: Her 50 questions: the right sheet came back for 34 (33 answers right, 1 not faithful) and the wrong year's sheet for 16 (15 faithful to it, 1 not). How many answers were faithful?
recall.why: Faithful means the answer stuck to the sheet it was handed, right year or not: the 33 right answers plus the 15 faithful to the wrong year, 33 + 15 = 48 of 50. Only 33 of those were right.

recall.prompt: An interviewer says: you've built an assistant for a client and tested it on 50 questions. Walk me through the report and the demo you'd bring to the meeting.

keyIdeas.idea: Lead with the number that answers the client's question, in the client's words
Define each metric beside its number and say who wrote the questions
Show three failures, say what the number does not mean, end with a recommendation
Run the demo on questions the client picks on the day, not only rehearsed ones

recall.model: I'd start with the client's question in their words and lead with the number that answers it: if they ask whether it can answer customers alone, the headline is right answers, out of 50. I'd define each metric in one plain sentence beside its number, and say who wrote the questions and from what. I'd show three failures in full, say what the number does not mean, and end with a recommendation they can act on. For the demo, the client picks the questions on the day; a rehearsed set only shows the cases I already know work.

recall.prompt: If faithfulness on her 50 were forced to 50 of 50 and the sheet-finding step left as it is, what is the most the right answers could reach?
recall.why: A faithful answer is only right if the sheet it stuck to was the right one. The right sheet came back for 34, so right answers stop at 34; the 16 wrong-year answers stay wrong, now more faithful to the wrong year.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. The merchant's staff check is still on, and his newsletter of Tuesday 8 December said what the test measured. In December I changed the finding step to match the year exactly before scoring. On Monday 1 February I started with a new client: a music shop, whose assistant will answer questions about instruments and repairs. A colleague had already written the design doc: 14 pages on how the system is built, which model it uses and how it finds the repair sheets. The owner will read it at Wednesday's meeting; on the phone he said: 'I just need to know what I'm signing up for.'
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What should the design doc give the owner, and in what order?

keyIdeas.idea: Lead with the decisions the owner must make, not how the system is built
Give each decision its options, what each costs and a recommendation
Put success in the owner's words, as a count with its denominator and each measure defined

coldCase.model: Turn it round: page 1 lists the decisions the owner must make, such as whether repair prices are answered or sent to staff, and whether anything is held for a person before it goes out. Give each decision two or three options, what each costs in speed, money and risk, and a recommendation. Then say what success means in his own words, as a count out of a stated number of questions, with each measure defined in a plain sentence. The 14 pages on how it's built go at the back.
